one_liner: Zero-allocation, path-based JSON field extractor for Go; 3-6.5x faster than encoding/json struct unmarshal on the project's benchmarks.
what_it_does: Extracts individual values from a JSON []byte by key path (Get(data, "person", "name"), with "[0]" for array indexes), so you do not define structs or decode into map[string]interface{}. Results come back as []byte slices into the original buffer plus a ValueType. The package also has typed helpers (GetString, GetInt, GetFloat, GetBoolean, GetUint64), iterators (EachArray, EachObject, and EachKey for many paths in one pass), experimental Set/Delete/Append, a lenient Config for single quotes and unknown escapes, and a streaming ReaderParser over io.Reader. It is not a drop-in replacement for encoding/json: there is no Unmarshal or Marshal, so each field access has to be rewritten.
how_it_is_fast: It never builds a tree. searchKeys walks the bytes once, tracks only nesting depth, compares keys in place, skips non-matching objects and arrays whole with a brace/bracket counter (blockEnd), and returns as soon as the path matches. String ends are found with an 8-byte SWAR (SIMD-within-a-register) scan for quote/backslash, and the hot loops use gjson's single-comparison fast skip (byte > 0x5C) over non-structural bytes. Values are sub-slices of the input, key comparison uses unsafe []byte-to-string casts, and escaped keys are unescaped into a 64-byte stack buffer, so extraction allocates nothing; EachKey matches all requested paths in one scan instead of rescanning per Get.
when_to_use: Pulling a few fields out of JSON whose schema is large, unknown or unstable (third-party API responses, log records), where defining structs for encoding/json is the cost you want to avoid.
GC-sensitive hot paths: Get and EachKey measured 0 B/op on all three benchmark payloads, versus 416-4,432 B/op for encoding/json struct unmarshal.

Reading several fields from one document with EachKey: one pass over the 2.4KB payload took 1,657 ns versus 9,911 ns for encoding/json, and it also beat gjson (2,241), easyjson (2,368) and sonic (2,703).
Arrays of records where you need one or two fields per element: EachArray plus Get on the 24KB payload took 20,114 ns versus 130,565 ns for encoding/json.
Multi-GB JSON files: ReaderParser reads from an io.Reader in 64 KiB chunks with a bounded sliding window (64 MiB by default) instead of loading the whole document.
when_not_to_use: You need most of the document as typed Go structs. There is no Unmarshal, and struct-binding libraries such as sonic (an encoding/json drop-in) or easyjson (code generation) fit that job better.
You need validation. Get stops at the first match and never checks the rest of the input, and getType labels any token starting with a digit or '-' as Number without checking its format.
Your code calls Get separately for each field on medium documents: on the 2.4KB benchmark Get (3,141 ns) was slower than gjson, easyjson and sonic, and only EachKey led.
You need decoded Go strings for most values. Get returns raw bytes with JSON escapes intact, and GetString/ParseString unescape but allocate, a cost the 0-alloc headline numbers leave out.
Your main job is writing or editing JSON. There is no encoder, and the README marks Set and Delete as experimental.

integration.dependencies: none (standard library only; go.mod has no require lines)
integration.min_toolchain: go.mod declares Go 1.13; CI runs Go 1.25; the published benchmarks used Go 1.26.3
integration.platforms: Any Go target: pure Go with no assembly files. Unsafe string/[]byte casts are the default, with a safe fallback under the appengine/tinygo build tags. The published benchmarks are arm64 only (Apple M4 Max).
integration.thread_safety: Not documented for the package-level functions. They keep no mutable package state (only read-only error values, literal byte slices and an escape table), so concurrent reads of a shared buffer appear safe. ReaderParser is documented as not safe for concurrent use and allows one operation per stream.

gotchas: Returned []byte values alias the input buffer. Capacity is clipped, so an append will not overwrite the input, but copy the values before you reuse or mutate the buffer. GetUnsafeString returns a string that stays valid only while the buffer lives and does not handle escapes.

Keys inside arrays are not searched unless you address the element with "[n]" or iterate with EachArray. When a key is duplicated, the first occurrence wins because searchKeys returns on the first match.

Use v1.5.1 or later. The v1.5.1 changelog fixes a stringEnd backslash scan that walked the rest of the document (128 us to 22 us on the 24KB payload). Versions up to v1.1.1 have denial-of-service advisories: CVE-2020-10675, CVE-2020-35381 and CVE-2026-32285, the last fixed in v1.1.2.

Seven releases (v1.3.0 to v1.6.1) shipped between 2026-07-27 and 2026-07-30 and added many APIs. Open issue #288 (filed 2026-08-04) reports that `go test` fails at HEAD on amd64 Linux (TestOracleSetPr286Regression) and that this blocks Debian packaging.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over gjson when allocations matter or you read many paths at once: in the repo's benchmarks jsonparser allocates 0 B/op everywhere against gjson's 64-28,672 B/op, and EachKey beats gjson on the small and medium payloads, though gjson's per-path Get is faster than jsonparser's Get at 2.4KB. Pick it over Sonic or easyjson only when you want a few fields rather than a typed struct, because those decode whole documents into structs.
verified_claims_summary: In the project's own benchmarks (Go 1.26.3, Apple M4 Max arm64, median of 5 `go test -bench` runs), reading username, id and slug from each array element of a 24KB Discourse-style payload took 20,114 ns/op with 0 allocations. encoding/json, unmarshalling into a minimal struct, took 130,565 ns/op with 147 allocations, a 6.5x gap. EachKey was about 5.7x faster on a 190B log record and about 6.0x faster on a 2.4KB record. The comparison is not like-for-like: jsonparser leaves values as undecoded []byte (the 0 B/op EachKey rows match the benchmark variants whose ParseString calls are commented out), while encoding/json builds Go strings.
status_note: Active (last commit 2026-08-21), MIT-licensed, standard-library-only and a single package, so it is easy to vendor. Still, pin a version and run your own tests, given the July 2026 burst of seven releases and the open report of failing tests at HEAD (#288).
